'''''Iris mesopotamica''''', the '''Mesopotamian iris''', is a species in the genus ''[[Iris (plant)|Iris]]'', it is also in the subgenus ''[[Iris subg. Iris|Iris]]''. It is a [[rhizomatous]] [[perennial plant|perennial]], from the middle East, within the countries of [[Iraq]], [[Turkey]], [[Syria]] and [[Israel]]. It has linear, grey-green or green broad leaves, tall stem with 2–3 branches, holding up to 9 scented flowers, in shades of violet, purple, lavender blue and light blue, with a yellow and white or orange and white beard. It is listed as a synonym of ''[[Iris × germanica]]'' in some sources. It is cultivated as an ornamental plant in [[temperateness|temperate]] regions, including being planted in graveyards and cemeteries but may also be used for celebrations and decoration.

==Description==
It is often confused with ''Iris trojana'' (now classed as a synonym of ''Iris × germanica'') and ''[[Iris cypriana]]''.<ref name=irisbotanique/> It is also similar in form to ''[[Iris cypriana]]'' but outer bract (spathe) is brown and papery in the upper third only.<ref name=European>James Cullen, Sabina G. Knees, H. Suzanne Cubey (Editors) {{Google books|CkxWrDqtWLQC|The European Garden Flora Flowering Plants: A Manual for the Identification (2011) |page=247}}</ref>

It is a [[geophyte]],<ref name=wild>{{cite web |title=Iris mesopotamica |url=http://www.wildflowers.co.il/english/plant.asp?ID=39 |publisher=wildflowers.co.il |access-date=30 October 2015}}</ref> that has thick rhizomes,<ref name=Avital>{{cite web|first=Avital |last=Ezer |title=Deer feces. Post Factum |date=26 May 2011 |url=http://aviezer.livejournal.com/6804.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180303071109/http://aviezer.livejournal.com/6804.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=3 March 2018 |publisher=aviezer.livejournal.com |access-date=31 October 2015 }}</ref><ref name=cgf>{{cite web |title=Genus Iris |url=http://www.cgf.net/plants.aspx?genus=IRIS |publisher=cgf.net |access-date=30 October 2015}}</ref> which are [[stolons|stoloniferous]], and semi-buried in the ground.<ref name=irisbotanique>{{cite web |title=Chapter I Rhizomatous Iris (part 2) |url=http://irisbotanique.over-blog.com/article-chapitre-i-les-iris-rhizomateux-partie-2-123788250.h |publisher=irisbotanique.over-blog.com |access-date=28 October 2015 |archive-date=28 May 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200528160300/http://irisbotanique.over-blog.com/article-chapitre-i-les-iris-rhizomateux-partie-2-123788250.h/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

It has linear,<ref name=wild/> green,<ref name=british>British Iris Society (1997) {{Google books|pL6uPLo7l2gC|A Guide to Species Irises: Their Identification and Cultivation|page=30}}</ref><ref name=vivaio>{{cite web |title=Iris mesopotamica |url=http://www.vivaiocorazza.com/en/products/599-iris-mesopotamica.html |publisher=vivaiocorazza.com |access-date=30 October 2015}}</ref> or grey-green,<ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=cgf/> glaucous leaves.<ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=british/><ref name=vivaio/>
The sheathing leaves,<ref name=irisbotanique/> can grow up to between {{convert|30|-|70|cm|0|abbr=on}} long,<ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=british/> and 5 cm wide.<ref name=british/><ref name=vivaio/> The leaves are wider than ''Iris cypriana''.<ref name=handbook>{{cite web |first=William |last=Dykes |author-link=William Rickatson Dykes  |title=Handbook of Garden Irises |year=2009 |url=http://www.beardlessiris.org/reviews/handbook%20of%20garden%20irises%20-%20dykes.pdf |publisher=beardlessiris.org (The Group for Beardless Irises) |access-date=1 November 2014}}</ref>

It has a tall stem,<ref name=signa>{{cite web |first=Ori |last=Fragman-Sapir |title=Iris mesopotamica |date=24 November 2007 |url=http://www.signa.org/index.pl?Iris-mesopotamica |publisher=signa.org (Species Iris Group of North America) |access-date=30 October 2015}}</ref><ref name=anenet>{{cite web |title=Mesopotamian Iris – Iris Mesopotamica |date=6 May 2011 |url=https://anenet110.wordpress.com/2011/05/06/איריס-ארם-נהריים-iris-mesopotamica/ |publisher=anenet110.wordpress.com |access-date=30 October 2015}}</ref> or [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]], that can grow up to between {{convert|90|-|150|cm|0|abbr=on}} tall.<ref name=american>{{cite web  |first=Bob |last=Pries |title=(SPEC) Iris mesopotamica Dykes |date=21 October 2015 |url=http://wiki.irises.org/bin/view/Spec/SpecMesopotamica  |publisher=wiki.irises.org (American Iris Society)| access-date=30 October 2015}}</ref><ref name=Norris>Kelly Norris {{Google books|6YwFZmzxgecC|A Guide to Bearded Irises: Cultivating the Rainbow for Beginners and Enthusiasts (2012) |page=119}}</ref><ref name=pacific>{{cite web |title=Iris summary |date=14 April 2014 |url=http://www.pacificbulbsociety.org/pbswiki/files/Iris/Iris_Summary.pdf |publisher=pacificbulbsociety.org |access-date=23 November 2014}}</ref><!--also<ref name=Avital/><ref name=anenet/><ref name=british/><ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=handbook/><ref name=vivaio/>--> It has 2 or 3 branched stems.<ref name=british/><ref name=cassidy>{{cite book |last1=Cassidy |first1=George E.| last2=Linnegar | first2=Sidney | date=1987 |edition=Revised  | title= Growing Irises  |location=Bromley | publisher=Christopher Helm | isbn=0-88192-089-4}}</ref>{{rp|123}}

The stem has broad,<ref name=british/><ref name=handbook/> [[Bract#Spathe|spathes]] (leaves of the flower bud), which are green in the lower half,<ref name=handbook/> and (scarious) membranous or brown and papery,<ref name=European/> in the upper third of the leaf.<ref name=british/>

The stems (and the branches) hold between 3 and 8,<ref name=Avital/><ref name=anenet/> or 9 flowers.<ref name=cassidy/>{{rp|123}} Each stem carries 2–3 flowers,<ref name=ClaireAustin/>{{rp|17}} at the terminal end of each branch,<ref name=british/> there is always a single flower per stem.<ref name=anenet/>
It blooms early in the season,<ref name=ClaireAustin>{{cite book |first=Claire |last=Austin |title=Irises; A Garden Encyclopedia |year=2005 |publisher=Timber Press |isbn=0881927309 }}</ref>{{rp|17}} between late spring and early summer,<ref name=European/> between May,<ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=tiuli>{{cite web |title=Mesopotamian Iris |url=http://www.tiuli.com/flower_info.asp?lng=eng&flower_id=425 |publisher=tiuli.com |access-date=2 November 2015}}</ref>
<ref name=Danin>{{cite web |first=Prof. Avinoam |last=Danin |title=Iris mesopotamica Dykes |url=http://flora.org.il/en/plants/IRIMES/ |publisher=flora.org.il (Flora of Israel Online) |access-date=30 October 2015}}</ref> and June.<ref name=cgf/><ref name=handbook/>

The large flowers,<ref name=Clutter>{{cite web |first=Jack |last=Clutterbuck |title=A Journey North |url=http://www.friendsjbg.org.uk/blogs |publisher=friendsjbg.org |access-date=31 October 2015}}</ref> are scented,<ref name=anenet/><ref name=cassidy/>{{rp|123}}<ref name=ClaireAustin/>{{rp|17}} and come in shades of violet,<ref name=british/><ref name=signa/><ref name=pacific/> purple,<ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=american/><ref name=ClaireAustin/>{{rp|17}}<!--also<ref name=Norris/><ref name=cgf/>--> lavender blue (similar in shade to ''[[Iris junonia]]''),<ref name=European/><ref name=handbook/> and light blue.<ref name=vivaio/><ref name=tiuli/> There are occasionally bi-toned flowers.<ref name=pacific/>

Like other irises, it has 2 pairs of petals,<ref name=wild/> 3 large [[sepals]] (outer petals), known as the 'falls' and 3 inner, smaller petals (or [[tepals]]), known as the 'standards'.<ref name=ClaireAustin/>{{rp|17}} The falls are obovate or cuneate (wedge shaped),<ref name=british/> with a white haft (section closest to the stem),<ref name=irisbotanique/> that has bronzy purple veins,<ref name=European/><ref name=Norris/><ref name=ClaireAustin/>{{rp|17}} or lines.<ref name=cgf/> In the centre of the fall, is a row of hairs called a beard, which are yellow,<ref name=vivaio/> or orange yellow,<ref name=irisbotanique/> at the base, turning white at the front of the petal.<ref name=European/><ref name=british/><ref name=vivaio/><ref name=ClaireAustin/>{{rp|17}} The standards are obovate or unguiculate (claw shaped), they are paler than the falls,<ref name=british/><ref name=ClaireAustin/>{{rp|17}} and have a pale haft that is also marked with bronzy-purple.<ref name=british/>

It has a {{convert|1.2|-|2|cm|0|abbr=on}} long perianth tube,<ref name=European/><ref name=british/> which is wider and shorter than the perianth tube of ''Iris cypriana''.<ref name=handbook/> It has a rounded ovary, blue-purple [[Stigma (botany)#Style|style arms]], violet crests, white filaments and cream anther.<ref name=british/>

After the iris has flowered, it produces an oblong or trigonal seed capsule, that is {{convert|5|-|6.5|cm|0|abbr=on}} long. Inside the capsule, are large, pyriform (pear-shaped), brown wrinkled seeds.<ref name=british/>

===Genetics===
As most irises are [[diploid]], having two sets of [[chromosomes]], this can be used to identify hybrids and classification of groupings.<ref name=ClaireAustin/>{{rp|18}}
''Iris mesopotamica'' is a tetraploid iris,<ref name=Norris/><ref name=cassidy/>{{rp|25}}<ref name=stebbings>{{cite book |last=Stebbings |first=Geoff |year=1997|title=The Gardener's Guide to Growing Irises |url=https://archive.org/details/gardenersguideto00steb|url-access=registration |location=Newton Abbot |publisher=David and Charles |pages=[https://archive.org/details/gardenersguideto00steb/page/28 28–29] |isbn=0715305395 }}</ref> which have developed from an [[autoploid]].<ref name=cyto>J. Schulz-Schaeffer {{Google books|w4juBwAAQBAJ|Cytogenetics: Plants, Animals, Humans (1980)|page=257}}</ref>
It was counted by Sturtevant and [[Lowell Fitz Randolph|Randolph]], in 1945,<ref name=cyto/> as 2n=48.<ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=pacific/><ref name=telp>{{cite web |first=Tom |last=Waters |title=A Hybridizer's Guide to Bearded Species |date=October 2010 |url=http://www.telp.com/irises/species.htm |publisher=telp.com |access-date=30 October 2015}}</ref><!--also<ref name=british/><ref name=stebbings/>-->

==Taxonomy==
It is commonly known as 'Mesopotamian Iris',<ref name=anenet/><ref name=tiuli/><ref name=Materia>[[Efraim Lev]] and Zohar Amar {{Google books|c62M1aMl6QUC|Practical Materia Medica of the Medieval Eastern Mediterranean According to the Cairo Genizah (2008)page=423}}</ref><!--also<ref name=wild/>--> or  '[[Aram-Naharaim|aram naharayim]] Iris',<ref name=Avital/> which is the old [[Hebrew]] word for [[Mesopotamia]].<ref>{{cite web |first=Aviva |last=Bar-Am |title=Wheel power in the north, a guide to the Norths wheelchair and stroller accessible sites |date=14 September 2009 |url=https://www.jpost.com/Israel-Guide/Northern-Israel-Tours/Wheel-power-in-the-north-A-guide-to-the-Norths-wheelchair-and-stroller-accessible-sites |publisher= jpost.com (The Jerusalem Post) |access-date= 31 October 2015}}</ref>

It is sometimes called 'Mardin Iris',<ref name=american/> which is also a common name for ''Iris × germanica''.<ref name=nowick>Elaine Nowick {{Google books|STTRCQAAQBAJ|Historical Common Names of Great Plains Plants, with Scientific Names Index (2015|page=221}}</ref>

It is known in Hebrew as אִירוּס אֲרַם-נַהֲרַיִם<ref name=wild/><ref name=anenet/><ref name=Danin/>
It is written in [[Arabic script|Arabic]] as أللّغة آلعربيّة	سوسن عراقي  <ref name=wild/>

The Latin [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] ''mesopotamica'' refers to the former region of Mesopotamia, which equates to the current countries of [[Iraq]], [[Syria]] and [[Kuwait]].

In the 1800s, Mr [[Michael Foster (physiologist)|Michael Foster]] was sent several rhizomes of wild plants collected in Turkey,<ref name="telp"/> and the eastern part of the Mediterranean.<ref name=efloras>{{cite web |title=FNA Vol. 26 Page 373, 375, 376 |url=http://efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200028171  |publisher=efloras.org (Flora of North America) |access-date=30 October 2015}}</ref> These included ''[[Iris cypriana]]'' Foster & Baker and ''Iris trojana'' A. Kerner ex Stapf.<ref name="stebbings"/>

Several iris rhizomes were then sent to Mr Dykes at [[Charterhouse School]] (in Surrey),<ref name=dykesonirises>{{cite web| first=William | last=Dykes |title=Dykes on Iris| url=http://www.beardlessiris.org/reviews/dykes%20on%20irises%20-%20part1.pdf |publisher=beardlessiris.org (The Group for Beardless Irises) | access-date=21 November 2014}}</ref> from [[Mardin]] in [[Armenia]],<ref name=handbook/> by another Charterhouse school teacher.<ref name=dykesonirises/> Some were later classified as ''[[Iris gatesii]]''
and others were then named and described as ''Iris mesopotamica'' by Dykes.<ref name=dykesonirises/>

It was first published and described by [[William Rickatson Dykes]] in his book, 'The Genus Iris' (Gen. Iris) page176 in 1913.<ref>{{cite web |title=Iridaceae Iris mesopotamica Dykes |url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=438870-1 |publisher=ipni.org (International Plant Names Index) |access-date=23 September 2015}}</ref><ref name=grin>{{GRIN | access-date=30 October 2015}}</ref>

It was also published in [[The Gardeners' Chronicle]] Vol.73 page237 on 21. October 1922 (with an illustration).<ref name=american/>

Later [[Brian Mathew]], then altered ''Iris × germanica'' to include other tall 48-chromosome tetraploids, including ''Iris cypriana'', ''Iris mesopotamica'', and ''Iris trojana''. ''[[Iris kashmiriana]]'' and ''[[Iris croatica]]'' are also connected with this group.<ref name=telp/>
Some authors still regard ''Iris mesopotamica'' as a form of ''Iris × germanica''.<ref name=Norris/><ref name="nowick"/> But others disagree.<ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=signa/><ref name=grin/>

It is not completely known whether this is a true natural species of iris or a cultivar.<ref name=noah>{{cite web |title=Mesopotamian iris |url=http://www.projectnoah.org/spottings/1562476012 |publisher=projectnoah.org |access-date=2 November 2015}}</ref>

In the iris trade, they are often confused with ''Iris cypriana'' and with ''Iris trojana'',<ref name=american/> (which is commonly listed as a synonym of ''Iris × germanica'').

It was verified by [[United States Department of Agriculture]] and the [[Agricultural Research Service]] on 4 April 2003 and then updated on 1 March 2007.<ref name=grin/>

It is listed in the [[Encyclopedia of Life]], as a synonym of ''Iris × germanica''.<ref name=eol>{{cite web |title=Iris × germanica
 |url=http://eol.org/pages/490948/names/synonyms  |publisher=eol.org |access-date=31 October 2015}}</ref>

It is listed as a synonym of ''Iris × germanica'' by [[The Plant List]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Iris × mesopotamica Dykes is a synonym of Iris × germanica L. |date= 23 March 2012 |url=http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/record/kew-322128  |publisher=theplantlist.org |access-date=30 October 2015}}</ref>

''Iris mesopotamica'' is listed as a synonym by the [[Royal Horticultural Society|RHS]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Iris mesopotamica |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/302067/i-Iris-mesopotamica-i/Details |publisher=www.rhs.org.uk| access-date=30 October 2015}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
It is [[native plant|native]] to Asia,<ref name=grin/> within the [[Middle East]],<ref name=vivaio/><ref name=Norris/><ref name=ClaireAustin/>{{rp|17}}<!--also<ref name=signa/><ref name=british/>--> or the [[Levant]],<ref name=cassidy/><ref name="Materia"/> (eastern Mediterranean,<ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=herbs>Thomas DeBaggio and Arthur O. Tucker {{Google books|7_KPgxEglHAC|The Encyclopedia of Herbs: A Comprehensive Reference to Herbs of Flavor and Fragrance (2009)|page=265}}</ref>).

===Range===
It is found in Turkey (including the region of [[Hatay Province]],<ref name=cgf/>),<ref name=European/><ref name=pacific/><ref name=grin/> Syria,<ref name=European/><ref name=pacific/><ref name=grin/> and Israel (within  [[Mount Hermon]],<ref name=Avital/><ref name=anenet/><ref name=Clutter/> [[Galilee]],<ref name=Avital/> and [[Golan]]<ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=wild/>).<ref name=European/><ref name=pacific/><ref name=grin/> It is [[endemic]] in Israel.<ref name=Avital/>

It was originally found in [[Armenia]],<ref name=handbook/> and [[Cyprus]],<ref name=cassidy/> but not any more.

[[Paul Mouterde]] (French botanist 1892–1972) stated that wild populations exist in the mountains of north Syria.<ref name=british/>

===Habitat===
It grows on dry rocky slopes,<ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=signa/> grasslands,<ref name=noah/> and on the semi-[[steppe]] [[shrubland]]s.<ref name=Danin/>

They can be found at an altitude of above {{convert|600|-|1400|m|ft|abbr=on}} above sea level.<ref name=Avital/>

==Conservation==
It was thought not to be growing wild,<ref name=british/><ref name=pacific/><ref name=ClaireAustin/>{{rp|17}} apart from in Israel.<ref name=signa/> Populations can be found on Mount Hermon,<ref name=signa/> where it is listed as common, on [[Mt. Gilboa]] and [[Valley of Springs Regional Council|Bet Shean Valley]], it is listed as V. Rare.<ref name=Danin/>

These populations are all protected.<ref name=Avital/><ref name=pacific/><ref name=tiuli/>

==Cultivation==
It is [[Hardiness (plants)|hardy]],<ref name=vivaio/> to European Zone H2,<ref name=European/> meaning Hardy to {{convert|-15|to|-20|C|F}}.<ref>{{cite web |title=Plant Hardiness |url=http://theseedsite.co.uk/hardiness.html |publisher=theseedsite.co |access-date=3 August 2015}}</ref> or RHS Hardiness Rating H5 ({{convert|-15|to|-10|C|F|disp=semicolon}}).<ref>{{cite web |first=Jim |last=Gardiner |title=New RHS hardiness ratings |date=February 2013 |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/about-the-rhs/publications/magazines/The-Garden/2013-issues/february/How-hardy-are-my-plants |publisher=rhs.org.uk |access-date=15 August 2015 |archive-date=4 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304084305/https://www.rhs.org.uk/about-the-rhs/publications/magazines/The-Garden/2013-issues/february/How-hardy-are-my-plants |url-status=dead }}</ref>

It prefers well drained soils,<ref name=irisbotanique/> but can tolerate heavy soils.<ref name=wild/>

It prefers positions in full sun.<ref name=irisbotanique/>

The rhizomes can be susceptible to 'iris root rot', also the leaves may also be affected by [[leaf spot]] (''heterosporium gracile'').<ref name=Farmers/>
The leaves can also be eaten by slugs and snails.<ref name=irisbotanique/>

Dykes recommends a planting time of between August and September.<ref name=handbook/>

It can be found for sale in some specialised nurseries, in Europe.<ref name=irisbotanique/>

===Propagation===
Irises can generally be propagated by [[Division (horticulture)|division]],<ref name=Avital/><ref>{{cite web |title=How to divide iris rhizomes |url=http://www.gardenersworld.com/how-to/projects/propagating/how-to-divide-iris-rhizomes/169.html |publisher=gardenersworld.com |access-date=12 October 2015 |archive-date=3 April 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160403230752/http://www.gardenersworld.com/how-to/projects/propagating/how-to-divide-iris-rhizomes/169.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> or by seed growing.<ref>{{cite web  |first=Mark S. |last=Porter |title=Montclair in full bloom |date=23 April 2013 |url=http://www.northjersey.com/community-news/montclair-in-full-bloom-1.693000?page=all |publisher=northjersy.com |access-date=30 October 2015}}</ref>

It sometimes produces tall seedlings with tall widely branching stems, that are sometimes too weak to hold up the flower.<ref name=Farmers>US Department of Agriculture  {{Google books|V3pHAQAAMAAJ|Farmers' Bulletin, Issues 1401–1425 (1928)|page=21}}</ref>

===Hybrids and cultivars===
[[Michael Foster (physiologist)|Michael Foster]] was the first to use the species in hybridisation.<ref name=cassidy/>{{rp|26}}<ref name=efloras/>  He crossed with ''Iris × germanica'' to create larger plants.<ref name=efloras/>  Then in the early 20th century, William Mohr,<ref name=historic>{{cite web |first=Sydney B. |last=Mitchell |title=Historic Tall Bearded Iris PURISSIMA |date=January 2014 |url= http://historiciris.blogspot.co.uk/2014/01/historic-tall-bearded-iris-purissima.html |publisher=historiciris.blogspot.co.uk |access-date=30 October 2015}}</ref> and Sydney B Mitchell (from California) used the iris in breeding programmes of tall bearded varieties.<ref name=Norris/>

The first tetraploid forms appeared in 1900, by 1943 there were up to 145 diploid, 23 triploid and 247 tetraploid cultivars.<ref name=Vainstein>A. Vainstein (Editor) {{Google books|6Qz9CAAAQBAJ|Breeding For Ornamentals: Classical and Molecular Approaches (2002)|page=98}}</ref>

Known ''Iris mesopotamica'' cultivars include Iris 'Ricardi' and Iris 'Ricardi Alba'.<ref name=american/>

Known ''Iris mesopotamica'' crosses include;
''[[Iris lutescens]]'' X ''Iris mesopotamica'' – 'Autumn Gleam'
''Iris mesopotamica'' X ''Iris × germanica'' – 'Eglamour', 'Father Time' and 'Mme. Claude Monet'
''Iris mesopotamica'' X ''[[Iris pallida]]'' – 'Andree Autissier', 'Blanc Bleute', 'Carthusian', 'Mlle. Jeanne Bel' and 'Mlle. Schwartz'
''[[Iris iberica]]'' X ''Iris mesopotamica''- 'Ib-Ric'.<ref name=american/>

Cultivar 'Purissima' (Stern 1946) comes from ''[[Iris cypriana]]'' x ''Iris pallida'' and Iris 'Juniata' x ''Iris mesopotamica''<ref name=Vainstein/>

==Toxicity==
Like many other irises, most parts of the plant are poisonous (rhizome and leaves), if mistakenly ingested can cause stomach pains and vomiting. Also handling the plant may cause a skin irritation or an allergic reaction.<ref>David G Spoerke and Susan C. Smolinske{{Google books|a7-f66fRfzQC|Toxicity of Houseplants|page=236}}</ref>

==Uses==
Iris mesopotamica has been used in the past in [[folk medicine]], for various uses including; treating animals bites and poisons, treating [[Haemorrhoids]] and sexual diseases, treating Internal diseases, treating [[inflammations]] and skin diseases.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Lev |first=Efraim |date=2002 |title=Reconstructed materia medica of the Medieval and Ottoman al-Sham |url=http://his.library.nenu.edu.cn/upload/soft/haoli/114/323.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170809092140/http://his.library.nenu.edu.cn/upload/soft/haoli/114/323.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-date=2017-08-09 |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology |volume=80 |issue=2–3 |pages=167–179 |doi=10.1016/s0378-8741(02)00029-6 |pmid=12007707 |access-date=31 October 2015 }}</ref>

The rhizomes also contain a plenty of [[starch]], including [[isoflavone]] and essential oils which are used in perfumery,<ref name=irisbotanique/> similar to ''[[Iris florentina]]''.

==Culture==
In the past, up to hundreds of years ago,<ref name=Avital/><ref name=anenet/> in the Levant,<ref name=Materia/> [[Arabs]],<ref name=Avital/> and [[Muslims]],<ref name=anenet/> planted ''[[Iris albicans]]'',<ref name=herbs/><ref name=Muslim>{{cite journal |last1=Dafni |first1=Amots |last2=Lev |first2=Efraim |last3=Beckmann |first3=Sabine |last4=Eichberger |first4=Christian |date=206 |title=Ritual plants of Muslim graveyards in northern Israel |url=http://www.ethnobiomed.com/content/pdf/1746-4269-2-38.pdf |journal=Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine |volume=2 |pages=38 |doi= 10.1186/1746-4269-2-38 |access-date=30 October 2015 |pmid=16961931 |pmc=1584233 |doi-access=free }}</ref> (another white flowering bearded iris) and ''Iris mesopotamica'' in cemeteries,<ref name=Clutter/> and graveyards,<ref name=noah/> beside the graves, as an ornamental.<ref name=signa/> Including in Israel, [[Palestine]], North Africa and Syria (since the 16th century).<ref name=Muslim/> Some graveyards and cemeteries were later abandoned, allowing the iris to become naturalised in some sites.<ref name=anenet/>
